units.zh: 武帝楊悼皇后既母養懷帝，后遇難時，懷帝尚幼，及即位，中詔述后恩愛。

translations.literal: Empress Yang Dao of Emperor Wu had already mother-nurtured Emperor Huai; when she later met violent death, Emperor Huai was still young; when he ascended, an inner edict recounted the empress's kindness and love.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang had raised the future Emperor Huai; when she was killed he was still a child, and on enthronement he issued a palace rescript praising her care.

units.zh: 及后祖載，群官議帝應為追制服，或以庶母慈己，依禮制小功五月，或以謂慈母服如母服齊衰者，眾議不同。

translations.literal: When later her funeral train departed, the many offices debated whether the emperor ought wear retroactive mourning—or some said because a concubine-mother had loved him, by ritual he should wear xiao gong five months—or some said foster-mother mourning like a mother's qi-cui—the many opinions differed.
translations.idiomatic: At her cortège the ministries split: some wanted retroactive weeds, some cited a nurturing concubine's xiao gong, some equated her to a legal mother in qi-cui.

units.zh: 閭丘沖議云：「楊后母養聖上，蓋以曲情。

translations.literal: Luqiu Chong debated: 'Empress Yang mother-nurtured the sage ascendant—generally out of special affection.
translations.idiomatic: Luqiu Chong debated: 'Empress Yang mother-nurtured the sage ascendant—generally out of special affection.

units.zh: 今以恩禮追崇，不配世祖廟。

translations.literal: Now by kindness and ritual we posthumously honor her—not pairing her in Emperor Shizu's temple.
translations.idiomatic: Now by kindness and ritual we posthumously honor her—not pairing her in Emperor Shizu's temple.

units.zh: 王者無慈養之服，謂宜祖載之日，可三朝素服發哀而已。」

translations.literal: For kings there is no garment for 'foster nurturing'; I say on the day of the funeral train, three court sessions in plain dress to raise mourning is enough.'
translations.idiomatic: For kings there is no garment for 'foster nurturing'; I say on the day of the funeral train, three court sessions in plain dress to raise mourning is enough.'

units.zh: 秦王天挺聖德，神武應期。

translations.literal: The Prince of Qin is heaven-endowed with sagely virtue, divine in arms and fitted to the hour.’
translations.idiomatic: The Prince of Qin bears heaven’s sagely virtue, a warlike spirit born for the moment.

translations.literal: He is a grandson of Emperor Shizu; you, Prince, are now the senior among us.
translations.idiomatic: You are of Shizu’s line, and among the princes you now stand first.

units.zh: 凡我晉人，食土之類，龜筮克從，幽明同款。

translations.literal: All of us people of Jin who live on this soil—tortoise-shell and milfoil approve, and the spirits of light and dark are of one mind.
translations.idiomatic: Every Jin subject dwelling on this earth finds tortoise and milfoil in accord, and both realms of the unseen give their assent.

units.zh: 漢之光武，不嗣于孝成，而上承於元帝。』

translations.literal: Han Guangwu does not succeed Xiaocheng but receives above from Emperor Yuan.
translations.idiomatic: Han's Guangwu does not follow Xiaocheng but inherits from Emperor Yuan.

units.zh: 又曰：『晉惠帝無後，懷帝承統，懷帝自繼于世祖，而不繼于惠帝。

translations.literal: Also: 'Jin Emperor Hui had no heir; Emperor Huai received the succession; Huai succeeded himself from Shizu, not from Emperor Hui.
translations.idiomatic: Jin Hui had no heir; Huai took the line from Shizu, not from Hui.

units.zh: 其惠帝當同陽甲、孝成，別出為廟。』

translations.literal: Emperor Hui should be the same as Yang Jia and Xiaocheng, separately enshrined outside.
translations.idiomatic: Hui should join Yang Jia and Xiaocheng in a separate shrine.

units.zh: 武皇帝諱炎，字安世，文帝長子也。

translations.literal: The Martial Emperor's taboo name was Yan, his style name Anshi; he was the eldest son of Emperor Wen.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor honored posthumously as Wu bore the personal name Yan and the courtesy name Anshi; he was the firstborn son of Emperor Wen (Sima Zhao).

units.zh: 己酉，帝崩于含章殿，時年五十五，葬峻陽陵，廟號世祖。

translations.literal: On the day jiyou the emperor died in the Hanzhang hall at age fifty-five; he was buried at Junyang mausoleum with temple name Shizu.
translations.idiomatic: Jiyou: the emperor expired in Hanzhang at fifty-five, buried at the Junyang tomb with the temple name Shizu.

decisions.reason: Jinshu 020 s0170 refers to the 世祖廟, the temple of 世祖. The supplied primary definition (Jinshu 003 s0636, 廟號世祖) states plainly that 世祖 is Sima Yan's temple name. So 'Emperor Shizu' is the English rendering of a temple name, and 'personal' was the wrong kind. The proposal changes only the kind; the English form, certainty and evidence stay the same.

In Jinshu 020 s0167 the name form is 武帝, as in 武帝楊悼皇后. This is not a personal name. Jinshu 003 s0001 opens with 武皇帝諱炎, which gives 炎 as his taboo (personal) name and sets it apart from the imperial designation 武(皇)帝. Jinshu 003 s0636 gives his temple name separately as 世祖. That leaves 武帝 as his posthumous imperial name, so posthumous-name is the right kind. Splitting the row keeps the correct contextual English personal name 'Sima Yan' as its own personal claim, deletes no alias, and keeps the certainty and evidence exactly as they were.

In Jinshu 020 s0170 the Chinese form is 世祖 (世祖廟). Jinshu 003 s0636 (廟號世祖) defines this as Sima Yan's temple name. The split classifies 世祖 as temple-name and keeps the correct English personal name 'Sima Yan' as a separate personal claim. The English identification does not need to repeat the Chinese spelling. Certainty and evidence are unchanged.

In Jinshu 086 s0102 (世祖之孫) the Western Jin founder appears under his temple name 世祖, which the context of a grandson heading the princes confirms. Jinshu 003 s0636 defines 世祖 as his temple name. The split classifies 世祖 as temple-name and keeps the correct English personal name 'Sima Yan' as a separate personal claim. Certainty and evidence are unchanged.

Jiutangshu 029 s0202 discusses Jin succession: 晉惠帝無後, and Emperor Huai 自繼于世祖 rather than 惠帝. Here 世祖 is the Jin founder, named by his temple name, and Jinshu 003 s0636 (廟號世祖) defines that temple name. 'Shizu' is the transliteration of that same temple name, so both the English and Chinese forms are correctly temple-name. The original row had no separate English personal name, so no split is needed. Certainty and evidence are unchanged.

whole114Renewal.reason: The earlier conclusion that all 114 members are the same person still holds, and no member is pruned. The only substantive change is to three member signatures (jinshu:020:p092, jinshu:086:p072 and jiutangshu:029:p125). Their name keys for 武帝, 世祖, 'Emperor Shizu' and 'Shizu' change kind from personal to posthumous-name or temple-name, and from blocking to nonblocking. I approved those five kind corrections against the primary Chinese. No name string, preferred name (Sima Yan / 司馬炎), role, family link, mention count or date hint is added or removed. The identity of these three members never rested on treating 世祖 or 武帝 as a personal name. It rests on the actual Chinese contexts. In Jinshu 020, Emperor Wu's empress Yang Dao raised 懷帝 and is not paired in the 世祖 temple. In Jinshu 086, the 世祖 whose grandson is addressed is a Jin ancestor of the 晉人. In Jiutangshu 029, 懷帝 is said to succeed 世祖 rather than 惠帝. Jinshu 003 ties these labels to one emperor: it names the annals subject as 武皇帝諱炎 and records 廟號世祖. So 世祖 (temple name) and 武帝 (posthumous name) both point to the Western Jin founder 炎, and the existing basis already chains them for the whole group (世祖武皇帝, 武帝受禪, the 惠帝/愍懷 family links). Reclassifying these labels as imperial names supports the merge; it does not weaken it. The other 111 signatures change only in renumbered claim-pointer provenance. I treat their hashes only as binding unchanged dependencies, not as new identity evidence, and the prior source-reviewed basis for them stands as before. The 79 candidate comparisons removed under the existing nonblocking temple/posthumous rules are all pairs of the merged Jin Wu cluster against other people. They remove no member and add no pair. The native validator reports that all prior canonical memberships are unchanged and that the strong-name evidence for all 114 members still passes, which agrees with this reading.
